main.summary: On hearing of the death of his nephew, the Twelfth, Han Yu wrote this funeral address. It recalls the years when uncle and nephew depended on each other, describes his grief, doubt and self-reproach at the news, gives arrangements for what must be done, and ends lamenting that they can never be together.
main.translation:
On such a year, month and day, your youngest uncle, Yu, seven days after hearing of your death, was at last able to swallow his grief and offer his sincerity, and sent Jianzhong to prepare from far away the delicacies of the season for an offering, to announce it to the spirit of you, Twelfth.
Alas! I lost my father young; by the time I was grown I could not remember the one I should have relied on, and depended only on my elder brother and his wife. In his middle years my brother died in the south. You and I were both small. We followed my sister-in-law to bury him at Heyang, and afterwards went with her to find a living in Jiangnan, forlorn and lonely, never apart for a single day. I had three elder brothers above me, all of whom, sadly, died young. Of those to carry on after our forefathers, in the generation of grandsons there was only you, and in the generation of sons only me. Two generations, one person each: a single form, a lone shadow. My sister-in-law once stroked you and pointed at me and said: 'Of two generations of the Han family, this is all that is left.' You were still small and cannot remember it; I, though I could remember, did not yet know how sad her words were.
At nineteen I first came to the capital. Four years later I went home to see you. Four years after that I went to Heyang to visit the family graves, and met you there, come with my sister-in-law's coffin for burial. Two years after that I was serving Prime Minister Dong at Bianzhou; you came to see me, stayed one year, and asked to go back and fetch your wife and children. The next year the minister died and I left Bianzhou, and you did not manage to come. That year I served in the army at Xuzhou; the men sent to fetch you had only just set out when I was dismissed again, and again you did not come. I thought that if you followed me in the east, the east too was a place for guests and could not last long; for a long-term plan, nothing was better than going back west, setting up a home, and then bringing you to it.
Alas! Who would have said that you would suddenly leave me and die! You and I were both young. I thought that though we were parted for a while, in the end we would live together for long. So I left you and lived as a guest in the capital, seeking a peck or two of salary. If I had truly known it would be like this, I would not have left you for a single day, even for the post of duke or minister with ten thousand chariots!
Last year, when Meng Dongye went to you, I wrote: 'I am not yet forty, yet my sight is blurred, my hair is grey, and my teeth are loose. I think of my uncles and elder brothers, all strong and healthy and yet dead early; one as worn as I am - can he last long? I cannot leave, and you are unwilling to come. I fear that I may die any morning or evening, and that you will carry a boundless grief.' Who would have said that the young would die and the old survive, that the strong would perish young and the sick remain whole?
Alas! Is it really so? Or is it a dream? Or is the report untrue? If it is so, can my brother's great virtue have had his heir cut short? Can your purity and brightness not have received its blessing? Can the young and strong die early, and the old and failing be whole and alive? It cannot be believed: it is a dream, the report is not true. But then why are Dongye's letter and Genglan's report lying here beside me? Alas! It is really so. My brother's great virtue has had his heir cut short; you, pure and bright, who ought to have carried on the family's work, did not receive its blessing. What men call Heaven is truly hard to fathom, and what they call the spirits are truly hard to understand; what they call principle cannot be worked out, and what they call a long life cannot be known.
Yet since this year my grey hair is turning white, my loose teeth are about to fall out, my body and blood grow weaker by the day, and my spirit fainter. How long before I follow you in death? If the dead have knowledge, how long will we be parted? If they have none, my sorrow will last only a short time, and the time without sorrow will have no end. Your son is just ten, mine just five. If the young and strong cannot be counted on, can I hope that such small children will grow up and stand on their own? Alas, the pity of it, the pity of it!
Your letter last year said: 'Lately I have caught the soft-leg disease, and it is often severe.' I said that this disease is common among the people of Jiangnan, and I never took it as a worry. Alas! Did it in the end take your life? Or was it some other illness that brought you to this? Your letter is dated the seventeenth of the sixth month; Dongye says you died on the second of the sixth month; Genglan's report gives no month or day. It seems that Dongye's messenger did not know to ask your household the date, and Genglan's report did not know it should state one; when Dongye wrote to me, he asked the messenger, who made something up to answer him. Is that so? Or not?
Now I am sending Jianzhong to make offerings to you, and to condole with your orphan and your nurse. If they have food enough to stay and wait out the mourning, let them wait until it is over and then bring them to me; if they cannot stay to the end, bring them at once. The other servants are all ordered to keep your mourning. When I have the means to rebury you, I will finally bury you in our ancestors' burial ground, and after that it will be as they wish.
Alas! When you fell ill I did not know the time; when you died I did not know the day. In life I could not look after you by living together; in death I could not hold your body and mourn to the full. At the coffining I did not lean on your coffin; at the burial I did not stand at your grave. My conduct has wronged the gods, and made you die young; unfilial and unkind, I could not live with you and care for you in life, nor stay by you in death. One of us at the edge of heaven, one at the corner of the earth: in life your shadow did not keep to my form, in death your soul does not meet my dreams. I did it myself, so whom can I blame? O blue Heaven, when will this reach its end! From now on I have no mind for this world. I shall look for a few tens of acres of land by the Yi and Ying rivers and wait out my remaining years there, teaching my son and yours, hoping they will grow up, and my daughter and yours, waiting for them to marry; that is all.
Alas! Words come to an end, but feeling cannot. Do you know it, or do you not? Alas, how sad! May you accept this offering.

keyLines.line: 吾少孤，及長，不省所怙，惟兄嫂是依
keyLines.en: I lost my father young, and when I grew up I had no memory of the father I should have leaned on; I depended only on my elder brother and his wife.
keyLines.note: He recalls losing his father as a child and being raised by his elder brother and sister-in-law, the background to the bond with his nephew.

keyLines.en: Two generations, one body each; a single shape, a lone shadow.
keyLines.note: It points out that of the Han family only two remained from two generations, alone and without support.

keyLines.en: Who would have said that you would so suddenly leave me and die?
keyLines.note: The first outburst of grief in the piece, a refusal to believe that his nephew has died so suddenly.

keyLines.line: 其信然邪？其夢邪？其傳之非其真邪
keyLines.en: Is it really true? Or is it a dream? Or is the news not true?
keyLines.note: Three questions in a row show his shock on hearing the news and his unwillingness to believe it.

keyLines.line: 所謂天者誠難測，而神者誠難明矣
keyLines.en: What they call Heaven is truly hard to fathom, and what they call the spirits are truly hard to understand.
keyLines.note: His grief turns to doubt about Heaven's will and the spirits, and a lament for the unfairness of the world.

keyLines.line: 汝病吾不知時，汝歿吾不知日，生不能相養於共居，歿不能撫汝以盡哀
keyLines.en: When you were ill I did not know the time, when you died I did not know the day; in life I could not support you living together, in death I could not hold you and mourn to the full.
keyLines.note: In a run of parallel phrases he regrets that he was at his side neither in illness nor in death, and his self-blame shows in every word.

keyLines.line: 一在天之涯，一在地之角，生而影不與吾形相依，死而魂不與吾夢相接
keyLines.en: One of us at the edge of heaven, one at the corner of the earth; in life your shadow did not follow my form, in death your soul does not meet my dreams.
keyLines.note: Through shadow and form, soul and dream, he writes the pain of being separated by life and death.

keyLines.line: 嗚呼！言有窮而情不可終
keyLines.en: Alas! Words have an end, but feeling cannot end.
keyLines.note: The close speaks straight from the heart: words run out, but grief cannot be finished.

glossary.note: A father's younger brother; Han Yu was the youngest of his brothers, so he calls himself ji fu.

glossary.en: shi xiu zhi dian - seasonal delicacies for offering
glossary.note: Fresh, choice food offered in season; xiu here is a variant of the character for 'delicacies'.
What one relies on; here, one's father.
One's wife and children. Read nu.

glossary.en: dou hu zhi lu - a peck or two of salary

glossary.note: Beriberi, caused by lack of vitamin B1, often seen in the south of the Yangtze in Tang times.
To lay a coffin in the grave. Read bian.

glossary.en: shang xiang - may you enjoy this
glossary.note: A closing formula of funeral addresses, hoping the dead will come and partake of the offering; xiang is a variant of the character for 'to enjoy'.

main.background: The funeral address to the Twelfth was written by Han Yu on hearing that his nephew Han Laocheng (the twelfth in his generation) had died, and is generally dated to 803. It does not follow the set form of a funeral address and speaks of deep feeling in everyday language, and it is regarded as the finest funeral address in the language.
